title: Undefined Behavior and Optimization Assumptions
learning_outcomes: Explain the main idea behind undefined behavior and optimization assumptions in your own words.
Apply undefined behavior and optimization assumptions to a minimal C example and predict the result.
Identify a relevant boundary, portability assumption, or failure mode.

content.intro: This lesson explores Undefined Behavior and Optimization Assumptions through an original visual, a compact C example and a check you can perform locally.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding undefined behavior and optimization assumptions helps you reason about C programs rather than relying on trial and error. It also helps you communicate assumptions, write safer code, and debug behavior across toolchains.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
Undefined Behavior and Optimization Assumptions is studied as part of **Performance, Optimization, and Profiling**. Start with the contract: identify the inputs or program state, the rule C applies, and the observable result. Then check the behavior in a small, repeatable example.

In C, details can depend on the selected language standard and implementation. Distinguish defined behavior from unspecified, implementation-defined, or undefined behavior, and consult the cited standard/compiler references when portability matters.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: For “Undefined Behavior and Optimization Assumptions”, write down the preconditions first. Identify valid inputs and boundaries, decide which C rule applies, then choose evidence that would falsify your assumption. Prefer a small test with a clear expected result and compile with diagnostics enabled.

content_blocks.title: Measure elapsed time
content_blocks.expected_output: Prints measured CPU time and a sink value; time varies by system.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This small example demonstrates a timing API, not a reliable benchmark. Use repeated trials, realistic workloads, and a profiler before optimizing.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, rebuild with the same compiler flags, rerun the same inputs, and compare actual output with the stated result. For time-, platform-, or input-dependent examples, record the environment and do not expect identical values everywhere.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf lesson page does not run C code. Compile locally or use a separately deployed, isolated C runner; do not execute arbitrary learner code inside FastAPI.

content_blocks.title: Portability and safety check
content_blocks.text: Use a documented standard mode; treat compiler extensions as extensions, not ISO C guarantees. Check return values, buffer bounds, and object lifetime. This course example is draft material and needs code review on the target toolchain before publication.

task: In a scratch file, create one small example that demonstrates undefined behavior and optimization assumptions. Explain the expected result before running it, compile with warnings enabled, and record one boundary case or portability question.
hints: Reduce the program to the smallest example that still shows the concept.
Write down the input, expected result, and assumptions before running it.
Check the official language/compiler reference and test a boundary case.
expected_output: A short, reproducible C example and explanation showing undefined behavior and optimization assumptions, plus a note about one boundary or portability consideration.
common_mistakes: Treating undefined behavior and optimization assumptions as a rule to memorize rather than a behavior to test.
Ignoring compiler warnings, input validity, or object lifetime.
Assuming behavior observed on one compiler is guaranteed by every C implementation.
